meta.title: Next.js App Router Guide
meta.description: An in-depth field guide to modern Next.js: routing, Server and Client Components, the RSC pipeline, data fetching, streaming, rendering, caching, mutations, security, SEO, performance, testing, and production.

hero.title: Build with Next.js without memorising magic.
hero.description: A field guide to the decisions that matter: where code runs, what crosses the server-client boundary, how routes are composed, when data is reused, and what actually reaches the browser.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.summary: Next.js gets easier once you stop treating it as a list of APIs and start following where work runs, what crosses the network, and what becomes interactive in the browser.

blocks.title: React describes the UI. Next.js coordinates the application.
paragraphs: React gives you components and a model for describing interfaces. Next.js adds the application around them: routing, server rendering, Server Components, data access, caching, request handling, asset optimisation, metadata, and build output.
The App Router is server-first. That does not mean every request renders the whole page on a server. It means code stays on the server unless the browser has a reason to own it.
blocks.note: A useful default is simple: keep work on the server until interaction requires the browser.

blocks.title: Follow one request
paragraphs: A visitor opens /projects. The router matches the URL to folders inside app, then combines the matching layouts and page into a component tree. Server Components can load data while that tree is rendered.

For the first visit, the browser receives HTML it can display plus React Server Component data that React uses to understand the server-rendered tree. Client Component JavaScript is loaded for the parts that actually need browser behaviour.
After that initial response, navigation can happen without replacing the whole document. Shared layouts stay mounted while the router fetches what the next route needs.
list: The URL chooses route segments.
Layouts compose the persistent shell.
Server Components do server-side work.
HTML gives the browser something useful to display immediately.
The RSC payload describes the server-rendered result and client references.
Client JavaScript hydrates the interactive boundaries.

blocks.title: A request from URL to interaction
blocks.code:
flowchart LR
    A[Browser requests /projects] --> B[Next.js Router]
    B --> C[Server Component tree]
    C --> D[(Database / API)]
    D --> C
    C --> E[HTML]
    C --> F[RSC payload]
    E --> G[Browser]
    F --> G
    H[Client JS chunks] --> G
    G --> I[Hydrate client boundaries]
    I --> J[Interactive UI]

blocks.title: Three questions solve most architecture choices
paragraphs: Before reaching for a directive or configuration option, decide what the feature actually needs. Most App Router decisions become much less mysterious after that.
list: Where must this code run: server, browser, or either?
How fresh must the result be: build-time, reusable for a while, or request-specific?
Does the user need to interact with it after the initial render?

blocks.title: A Next.js app does not need one rendering mode
paragraphs: Do not label an entire application as static or dynamic too early. A mostly static page can contain a dynamic region. A dynamic route can reuse cached work. A slow section can stream without delaying the rest of the page.
Think about the smallest useful boundary: route, component, query, or mutation.

sections.title: Routing and special files
sections.summary: The app directory is both a URL tree and a UI composition tree. The special files around a route describe how it loads, fails, and shares layout.

blocks.title: Read app as a route tree
paragraphs: A page.tsx makes a segment reachable. A layout.tsx wraps that segment and its descendants. Nested folders create nested URL segments, while route groups organise code without appearing in the URL.
The useful part of nested routing is not the folder syntax itself. It is that shared UI can live at the level where it actually belongs.
blocks.code:
app/
├─ layout.tsx
├─ page.tsx
├─ (marketing)/
│  ├─ about/page.tsx
│  └─ projects/
│     ├─ page.tsx
│     └─ [slug]/page.tsx
├─ dashboard/
│  ├─ layout.tsx
│  ├─ loading.tsx
│  ├─ error.tsx
│  └─ settings/page.tsx
└─ api/projects/route.ts

blocks.title: The files worth remembering
list: page.tsx exposes UI for a route.
layout.tsx wraps a segment and descendants while preserving shared UI across navigation.
template.tsx is similar to a layout but creates a new instance on navigation.
loading.tsx supplies a route-level Suspense fallback.
error.tsx catches uncaught runtime errors for a segment and is a Client Component.
global-error.tsx is the last error boundary around the root layout.
not-found.tsx renders missing-resource UI.
route.ts creates an HTTP Route Handler.
default.tsx supplies a fallback for unmatched parallel-route slots.

blocks.title: Dynamic segments are for resource identity
paragraphs: Use [slug] when a URL segment identifies a resource. Catch-all segments such as [...slug] can represent a path of arbitrary depth, while [[...slug]] also allows the empty case.
Do not force every piece of state into the pathname. Resource identity usually belongs in segments; sorting, filtering, search, and pagination often fit search parameters better.
blocks.code:
app/projects/[slug]/page.tsx       // /projects/project-a
app/docs/[...segments]/page.tsx      // /docs/react/server
app/shop/[[...category]]/page.tsx    // /shop or /shop/shoes

blocks.title: Route groups organise without changing the URL
paragraphs: A folder wrapped in parentheses is omitted from the public URL. app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx still maps to /about.
They are useful for code organisation and layout boundaries. They are not an access-control mechanism.

blocks.title: Parallel and intercepting routes solve specific UI problems
paragraphs: Parallel routes use named slots such as @activity to render independently routed regions in one layout. Intercepting routes let navigation display another route inside the current context, such as opening a photo in a modal from a gallery while keeping the photo URL directly addressable.
Both are useful when the interaction genuinely needs routing semantics. They also make the route tree harder to reason about, so ordinary nested routes should remain the default.

sections.title: Server and Client Components
sections.summary: The server-client boundary decides where code executes, what JavaScript ships, and which values are allowed to cross into the browser.

blocks.title: Start on the server
paragraphs: Pages and layouts are Server Components by default. They can read from a database, call private services, use server-only environment variables, and render without shipping their component implementation as normal browser JavaScript.
That makes Server Components a good home for work the browser does not need to own.

blocks.title: 'use client' is a boundary, not a decoration
paragraphs: The directive marks an entry point into the client module graph. Imports below that boundary may become part of the client bundle. Putting it on a large page because one button needs onClick can therefore move much more code to the browser than intended.
Extract the interactive part instead. Let the page stay on the server and give the browser the smallest useful client component.

blocks.title: Use the client when the browser owns the behaviour
list: Local state with useState or useReducer.
Event handlers such as onClick and onChange.
Effects.
DOM and browser APIs such as localStorage, Canvas, navigator, ResizeObserver, and media APIs.
Client-side context providers.
Custom hooks that depend on client-only React APIs.

blocks.title: Crossing the boundary changes what you can pass
paragraphs: Data passed from a Server Component into a Client Component crosses a serialization boundary. Prefer plain data supported by React's server-client protocol.
Do not try to pass database clients, secret-bearing service objects, arbitrary class instances, or browser-incompatible objects across that line.

blocks.title: A client shell can still receive server-rendered content
paragraphs: A Client Component can accept server-rendered content through props such as children. That pattern is useful when the wrapper needs interaction but the content inside it does not.
Think in boundaries rather than whole pages. A small client island can sit inside a much larger server-rendered tree.

sections.title: The RSC rendering pipeline
sections.summary: HTML, the RSC payload, and client JavaScript have different jobs. Once those jobs are clear, hydration and App Router navigation make much more sense.

blocks.title: Three pieces arrive for different reasons
list: HTML gives the browser a useful initial representation.
The RSC payload describes rendered Server Component output and references to Client Components.
Client JavaScript provides the implementation needed to hydrate and run interactive components.

blocks.title: The RSC payload is not HTML
paragraphs: React uses a framework-managed serialized representation for Server Component output. It lets React reconcile the server-rendered tree and understand where Client Components belong.
The important consequence is architectural: a Server Component can contribute UI without its implementation becoming ordinary client-side application code.

blocks.title: From component tree to interactive page
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
    A[React component tree] --> B{Component type}
    B -->|Server| C[Render on server]
    B -->|Client| D[Create client reference]
    C --> E[RSC payload]
    D --> E
    C --> F[Initial HTML]
    E --> G[Browser]
    F --> G
    H[Client JS chunks] --> G
    G --> I[Reconcile tree]
    I --> J[Hydrate client boundaries]

blocks.title: Hydration is where interaction wakes up
paragraphs: Server-rendered HTML can be visible before every interactive component is ready. Hydration attaches React's client behaviour to the relevant markup.
This is one reason client bundle size still matters in a server-first application. Unnecessary client boundaries mean more code to download, parse, execute, and hydrate.

sections.title: Data fetching
sections.summary: Fetch data where it is needed, keep server data on the server when possible, and watch for accidental waterfalls.

blocks.title: Server Components can go straight to the source
paragraphs: An async Server Component can call fetch, an ORM, or a database function directly. You do not need to create an internal HTTP endpoint just to get data from your own server into your own Server Component.
In current App Router behaviour, fetch requests are not something you should assume are cached by default. Make reuse and freshness explicit.

blocks.title: Sequential awaits can quietly become a waterfall
paragraphs: If request B does not depend on request A, waiting for A before starting B only adds latency. Start independent work together.
This matters more as pages accumulate small service calls. Three harmless-looking awaits can turn into a noticeably slow route.
blocks.code:
const [profile, projects, activity] = await Promise.all([
  getProfile(),
  getProjects(),
  getActivity(),
])

blocks.title: Colocate reads with the component that needs them
paragraphs: A giant page-level data loader is not automatically cleaner. Server Components make it practical for a section to own the query it needs.
Colocation works best when shared data access lives in reusable server functions, so the component owns the decision to fetch without duplicating domain logic.

blocks.title: Separate components do not justify duplicate expensive work
paragraphs: If multiple parts of a render need the same expensive computation or database result, make reuse deliberate. The exact mechanism depends on whether you need request-local deduplication or persistent caching.
Do not add a global cache merely because two components happen to call the same function. First decide the lifetime and invalidation semantics you actually need.

sections.title: Streaming and Suspense
sections.summary: Streaming lets useful parts of a route arrive before slower work finishes. Suspense is the boundary that makes that reveal sequence explicit.

blocks.title: Do not make the whole page wait for its slowest section
paragraphs: A page heading, navigation, and core product information may be ready immediately while recommendations take another second. Without a boundary, the slow region can delay everything around it.
Streaming lets the stable shell arrive first and fills slower regions as they resolve.

blocks.title: loading.tsx gives a route an instant fallback
paragraphs: A loading.tsx file creates a Suspense boundary around the route segment. It is a good default for navigation where the next page may need server work before its content is ready.
Keep the fallback structurally close to the final layout so the page does not jump around when content appears.

blocks.title: Use Suspense when only part of the page is slow
A boundary is a UX decision
paragraphs: Do not wrap every component in Suspense just because you can. Group content that should appear together and split content that can meaningfully arrive later.
The right boundary usually follows how a person reads the page, not how the files happen to be organised.

sections.title: Rendering strategies
sections.summary: Static, dynamic, cached, and streamed are not competing application types. They are tools you can combine at the boundary that needs them.

blocks.title: Static work is a good fit for stable public content
paragraphs: Documentation, portfolio pages, public articles, and stable marketing content are good candidates for reusable output. If the result does not depend on each request, repeating the work for every visitor is wasteful.
Static rendering is about when output can be produced and reused. It does not automatically mean the browser will keep the HTML forever.

blocks.title: Dynamic work exists because the request matters
paragraphs: Account state, request-specific headers, permissions, and genuinely real-time information can require work at request time. That is not a failure to optimise; sometimes freshness and identity are part of the feature.
Keep the dynamic boundary as narrow as the product allows.

blocks.title: Most interesting pages are mixed
paragraphs: A product page may have reusable product copy, cached reviews, and a request-specific cart indicator. Treating the entire route as one freshness unit throws away useful flexibility.
Cache Components are designed around this idea: stable work can be reused while runtime work remains dynamic.

blocks.title: Choose by dependency, not fashion
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
    A[Does output depend on this request?] -->|No| B[Can it be reused?]
    A -->|Yes| C[Render dynamically]
    B -->|Yes| D[Prerender or cache]
    B -->|No| C
    D --> E[Invalidate when freshness requires]
    C --> F[Use Suspense if slow regions can stream]

sections.title: Caching and freshness
sections.summary: Caching is a promise about acceptable staleness. Browser caching, CDN caching, and cached application work are different promises.

blocks.title: Start with acceptable staleness
paragraphs: Do not cache something just because it is expensive. First decide how stale the result is allowed to become. Documentation may tolerate long reuse; inventory may tolerate seconds; permissions may need request-time truth.
Once the freshness requirement is clear, choose the smallest cache boundary that satisfies it.

blocks.title: Do not confuse the layers
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
    A[Browser] --> B[Browser HTTP cache]
    B --> C[CDN / edge cache]
    C --> D[Next.js application]
    D --> E[Cached computation / data]
    D --> F[(Database / API)]
    E --> D
    F --> D

blocks.title: Static rendering is not browser caching
paragraphs: Static rendering answers when route output can be produced and reused. HTTP caching answers whether a browser or intermediary may reuse a response without fetching or revalidating it.
That is why a statically rendered page can still return browser-facing Cache-Control that requires revalidation while the hosting layer serves the route from its own cache.
blocks.note: A CDN cache HIT and browser max-age=0 are not contradictory. They describe different layers.

blocks.title: Cache reusable work deliberately
paragraphs: With Cache Components enabled, 'use cache' marks work whose result can be reused. cacheLife describes its lifetime and cacheTag gives related data a domain name that mutations can invalidate.
The useful cache boundary is often smaller than a route. Stable sections can be reused while request-specific sections remain dynamic.

blocks.title: Invalidate by meaning when you can
list: revalidateTag(tag, 'max') fits stale-while-revalidate behaviour.
updateTag(tag) is useful after a Server Action when the writer should immediately see fresh data.
revalidatePath(path) refreshes by route when a precise domain tag is not available.
Prefer tags such as projects or project:123 over names tied to a component.

blocks.title: Shared caches and personalised data are a dangerous mix
paragraphs: Do not put permission-sensitive or user-specific output into a shared cache unless the cache key and framework semantics truly isolate every value that changes the result.
Authentication state, ownership checks, tokens, and secrets should make you conservative. A fast response is not worth serving one user's data to another.

blocks.title: Do not mix caching models from different Next.js eras
paragraphs: Older tutorials often describe caching through a different set of defaults and route-level concepts. Current Cache Components documentation uses 'use cache', cacheLife, and cacheTag as the central model when the feature is enabled.
When maintaining an existing project, check its Next.js version and next.config.ts before copying a caching example from a newer guide.

sections.title: Mutations and Server Actions
sections.summary: Server Actions make server mutations convenient, but convenience does not remove validation, authentication, authorisation, or error handling.

blocks.title: Treat every Server Action like an exposed server operation
paragraphs: A button being hidden does not protect the operation behind it. Validate the input and check the caller inside the action or inside the server-side domain function it invokes.
A reliable mutation sequence is boring on purpose: authenticate, authorise, validate, write, invalidate, then redirect or return a typed result.

blocks.title: Keep the write path obvious
Validation errors are normal results
paragraphs: Bad form input is not an infrastructure failure. Return field-level information the UI can display near the relevant control instead of throwing everything into an error boundary.
Reserve thrown exceptions for failures the current flow cannot reasonably handle.

blocks.title: Forms are still useful without turning everything into client state
paragraphs: Server Actions work naturally with forms. Keep the server mutation independent from cosmetic client behaviour, then add pending state and optimistic UI only where they improve the experience.
Do not build a client-side state machine for a simple form just because the framework allows one.

sections.title: Route Handlers
sections.summary: Use route.ts when HTTP is the boundary you actually need: public APIs, webhooks, callbacks, feeds, files, and external integrations.

blocks.title: Create an HTTP boundary for an HTTP consumer
paragraphs: Route Handlers support standard HTTP methods and Web Request/Response APIs. They are a natural fit when a browser, mobile app, webhook provider, or another service needs an HTTP endpoint.
They are not a compulsory middle layer between a Server Component and your own database.

blocks.title: Do not fetch your own API just because it exists
paragraphs: If a Server Component and a Route Handler eventually need the same query, put that query in a shared server-side function. Let both entry points call it.
Sending the Server Component through HTTP first adds serialization, networking, error handling, and another boundary without necessarily adding value.

blocks.title: Pick the boundary based on the caller
list: Server Component needing internal data → call the server data/service layer directly.
Form mutation → often a Server Action.
External webhook → Route Handler.
OAuth callback → Route Handler.
Public JSON API → Route Handler.
Generated feed or file response → Route Handler.

sections.title: Proxy and request interception
sections.summary: Proxy runs before a matching route and is useful for request-level decisions. It should stay thin.

blocks.title: Think of Proxy as a request gate, not your application layer
paragraphs: Modern Next.js uses the Proxy convention for work that happens before a request reaches the route. Older material may call the same broad concept middleware.
Good uses include redirects, rewrites, lightweight header changes, and routing decisions that genuinely need to happen before rendering.

blocks.title: Where Proxy sits
blocks.code:
flowchart LR
    A[Browser] --> B[CDN / platform]
    B --> C[proxy.ts]
    C -->|redirect| D[Another URL]
    C -->|rewrite / continue| E[Next.js route]
    E --> F[Server Components or Route Handler]

blocks.title: A redirect is not an authorisation boundary
paragraphs: Proxy can improve navigation by redirecting obviously unauthenticated requests, but protected data still needs server-side permission checks close to the operation that reads or changes it.
Other entry points may reach the same data without going through the UI path you had in mind.

blocks.title: Keep it cheap
paragraphs: Code in the request path runs often. Avoid turning Proxy into a second application with database-heavy business logic and complicated branching.
If a decision can happen safely inside the route or data-access layer, that is often easier to test and maintain.

sections.title: Errors, loading, and recovery
sections.summary: Failure is part of the interface. Put boundaries close enough to the work that one broken region does not erase everything around it.

blocks.title: Give each meaningful route a recovery plan
paragraphs: loading.tsx handles waiting, error.tsx handles unexpected failures in a segment, not-found.tsx handles missing resources, and global-error.tsx is the final boundary around the root.
A recommendations failure should not remove the product title and purchase controls. Boundary placement should follow what can fail independently.

blocks.title: A recoverable error can offer retry
Expected errors are data
paragraphs: Validation failures, unavailable inventory, and rejected permissions are expected outcomes. Return them in a shape the UI understands.
Throw when the current code cannot meaningfully continue, not simply because a result is negative.

blocks.title: Log enough context to debug, not enough to leak
list: Include route, operation, correlation/request identifiers, and safe domain identifiers.
Do not log passwords, tokens, session cookies, raw secrets, or unnecessary personal data.
Make retries idempotent when the same operation may run more than once.
Test empty, loading, error, and missing-resource states before production.

sections.title: Authentication and security
sections.summary: Authentication tells you who is calling. Authorisation decides what that caller is allowed to do. The second check is where many applications get careless.

blocks.title: Signed in does not mean allowed
paragraphs: A valid session proves identity. It does not prove ownership of a project, access to an organisation, or permission to perform an administrative action.
Check permissions at the server operation that touches protected data.

blocks.title: Put security close to the data
paragraphs: Server Actions, Route Handlers, and server-side data functions should enforce the permissions they rely on. Layout checks and hidden controls can improve UX, but they are not enough by themselves.
Keeping these checks close to data access also makes it harder for a future entry point to accidentally bypass them.

blocks.title: NEXT_PUBLIC_ means public
paragraphs: Server-only environment variables can hold secrets. Variables intentionally exposed with NEXT_PUBLIC_ can enter browser bundles and must be treated as public information.
The prefix does not make a secret safe. It does the opposite: it tells the build that the value is allowed on the client.
blocks.code:
DATABASE_URL=...             # server only
AUTH_SECRET=...              # server only
NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID=... # intentionally public

blocks.title: The boring controls still matter
list: Validate untrusted input on the server.
Check resource ownership and roles.
Use secure, HTTP-only, same-site cookies where appropriate for session identifiers.
Protect state-changing operations from cross-site abuse.
Rate-limit expensive or sensitive public endpoints.
Return only the fields the client actually needs.
Keep dependencies and the framework patched.

sections.title: Metadata and SEO
sections.summary: SEO starts with pages that are understandable, crawlable, fast, and worth reading. Metadata helps describe those pages; it does not replace them.

blocks.title: Give each public route a specific identity
paragraphs: Use static metadata for fixed pages and generateMetadata when values depend on route data. Titles and descriptions should describe the page people are actually landing on, not repeat one site-wide string everywhere.
Set a canonical host, use route-specific Open Graph images where they add value, and keep important content present in server-rendered HTML.

blocks.title: Use the root for defaults, not every page's final copy
paragraphs: The root layout is a good place for metadataBase, a title template, authorship, default social images, and other site-wide defaults. Individual routes can then provide the part that is actually unique.
This keeps metadata consistent without turning every page into a clone of the homepage.

blocks.title: Make discovery boring and reliable
list: Expose canonical public URLs in sitemap.xml.
Use robots.txt intentionally; do not rely on it as an access-control system.
Use permanent redirects when a public URL moves.
Keep internal links crawlable.
Return meaningful HTML and successful status codes for real public pages.
Use noindex for pages that should not appear in search.

blocks.title: Structured data should describe visible reality
paragraphs: JSON-LD can help machines understand entities such as a Person, WebSite, Article, or BreadcrumbList. It should match content a visitor can actually see.
For a personal engineering site, Person and WebSite data are useful global foundations, while article-specific structured data belongs on the article itself.

blocks.title: Metadata cannot rescue thin content
paragraphs: A useful technical article that answers a real question has far more search value than a page stuffed with keywords. Write the page for the person who has the problem, then make its metadata accurately describe that page.
Good internal linking also matters: a caching article can point to a performance guide, a project case study, and a related tool without forcing the reader back through the homepage.

sections.title: Images, fonts, and scripts
sections.summary: Assets affect loading more than their file size suggests. Images can move layout, fonts can delay text, and third-party scripts can steal main-thread time.

blocks.title: Use next/image when its optimisation model fits
paragraphs: Image handles sizing and optimisation concerns that are easy to get wrong by hand. Always give the browser enough sizing information to reserve space and avoid layout shift.
For remote images, keep the allowed hosts and path patterns as narrow as practical.

blocks.title: Treat the hero image differently from the tenth image
paragraphs: The image that becomes Largest Contentful Paint may need earlier discovery and loading. Images below the fold usually should not compete with it.
Do not mark every image as high priority. Priority stops being useful when everything has it.

blocks.title: Fonts are part of rendering performance
paragraphs: next/font can self-host font files and reduce the need for separate third-party font requests. Keep the number of families, weights, and styles deliberate.
A design rarely needs every weight a font offers.

blocks.title: Third-party JavaScript deserves suspicion
paragraphs: Analytics, embeds, chat widgets, and marketing scripts can affect responsiveness long after your own bundle is optimised. Load them according to when they are actually needed.
Measure their effect in production instead of assuming a small snippet has a small runtime cost.

sections.title: Performance
sections.summary: Performance is mostly the result of architecture: how much work you do, where you do it, when you do it, and how much JavaScript you ask the browser to own.

blocks.title: The cheapest client JavaScript is the JavaScript you never send
paragraphs: Server Components give you a structural way to keep non-interactive code out of the browser bundle. That is often more valuable than shaving a few bytes from code that never needed to be client-side in the first place.
Audit large 'use client' boundaries before reaching for micro-optimisations.
blocks.code:
Large client boundary
        ↓
More modules enter client graph
        ↓
More JS downloaded and parsed
        ↓
More code to execute and hydrate
        ↓
Potentially slower interaction

blocks.title: Know what the Core Web Vitals are telling you
list: LCP is about how quickly the main visible content appears.
INP reflects responsiveness to user interaction.
CLS measures unexpected visual movement.
Use field data when available. A perfect local run is not the same as real users on real devices.

blocks.title: Network shape often matters more than raw query speed
paragraphs: A 100 ms request followed by another 100 ms request is slower than starting both together when they are independent. Look for waterfalls in server work, browser requests, fonts, images, and third-party scripts.
Streaming can improve perceived speed when some work cannot be made faster or parallel.

blocks.title: Prefetch with intent
paragraphs: Next.js navigation can prefetch route data to make transitions feel immediate. That is useful, but prefetching still consumes network and server resources.
For unusually large or expensive destinations, test the trade-off instead of assuming more prefetching is always better.

blocks.title: Optimise from evidence
paragraphs: Use production traces, Web Vitals, bundle information, database timings, and request waterfalls to find the real bottleneck. Performance work based only on intuition tends to optimise whatever is easiest to see.
The fastest component is irrelevant if the route is waiting on a serial database waterfall.

sections.title: Application architecture
sections.summary: Next.js tells you how routes work. It does not require every domain rule, database query, and UI component to live beside page.tsx.

blocks.title: Keep routing thin enough to see the application
blocks.code:
src/
├─ app/
│  ├─ (marketing)/
│  ├─ dashboard/
│  ├─ api/
│  └─ layout.tsx
├─ features/
│  ├─ projects/
│  │  ├─ components/
│  │  ├─ actions.ts
│  │  ├─ queries.ts
│  │  └─ schema.ts
│  └─ users/
├─ components/
│  └─ ui/
├─ lib/
│  ├─ auth/
│  ├─ db/
│  └─ utils/
└─ types/

blocks.title: This is a convention, not a Next.js requirement
paragraphs: Small applications do not need a large architecture diagram. Colocation is often clearer until a feature grows enough to deserve its own boundary.
The goal is to make ownership obvious, not to create folders for every noun.

blocks.title: Separate transport from domain work
paragraphs: A Server Action, Route Handler, and Server Component may all need the same business operation. Put the reusable domain or data logic below those entry points rather than duplicating it in each transport.
That also makes testing easier: the core rule can be tested without pretending every call came through HTTP.

blocks.title: Make server-only assumptions explicit
paragraphs: Database clients, secret-bearing SDKs, and privileged service functions should stay in modules that are clearly server-side. Do not rely on everyone remembering which utility is safe to import into a Client Component.
Clear module boundaries are cheaper than debugging an accidental client bundle leak later.

sections.title: Testing strategy
sections.summary: Test behaviour at the cheapest level that gives confidence, then use browser tests for the journeys that only make sense as a whole.

blocks.title: Different failures need different tests
paragraphs: Pure transformations, validation, and domain rules are cheap to unit test. Integration tests are better for database access, authentication, caching, and mutations working together. End-to-end tests protect a small number of critical user journeys.
Do not force every async Server Component through a client-oriented component harness if an integration test explains the behaviour more naturally.

blocks.title: Mutation tests should include the unhappy paths
list: Authenticated and unauthenticated callers.
Authorised and unauthorised resources.
Valid and invalid input.
Successful writes and expected conflicts.
Cache invalidation after the write.
Idempotency where retries are possible.

blocks.title: Test the states users actually see
list: Loading.
Empty.
Success.
Validation failure.
Unexpected error.
Not found.
Slow network where timing changes the experience.

blocks.title: Development mode is not production
paragraphs: Run tests against a production build for the flows where bundling, caching, routing, or server behaviour matters. Development mode deliberately behaves differently in several areas.
CI should at least catch type errors, lint failures, test failures, and a broken production build before deployment.

sections.title: Deployment and observability
sections.summary: A green deployment only proves the build finished. Production confidence comes from knowing what the application does after real traffic arrives.

blocks.title: Understand what your hosting platform is doing for you
paragraphs: Next.js can run in different deployment environments, but caching, image optimisation, runtime support, and server behaviour depend on how the platform implements them.
If you self-host, read the deployment guidance instead of assuming a Node process behind a reverse proxy behaves exactly like a managed Next.js platform.

blocks.title: Inspect the real response
paragraphs: Check headers, redirects, canonical URLs, cookies, robots.txt, sitemap.xml, and caching on the deployed domain. Local assumptions are not evidence of production behaviour.
For caching problems, identify which layer a header describes before concluding that the page is or is not cached.

blocks.title: Monitor the things that hurt users
list: Unhandled server and client errors.
Slow routes and slow database queries.
Core Web Vitals.
Failed Server Actions and Route Handlers.
External API latency and failures.
Background jobs if the application uses them.
Unexpected cache misses or stale-data incidents where relevant.

blocks.title: Logs should help answer a question
paragraphs: A wall of console output is not observability. Use structured context so a production error can be connected to a route, operation, and request without exposing sensitive data.
Add correlation identifiers when one user action crosses several services.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.summary: Most App Router problems are not caused by obscure APIs. They come from using a familiar pattern in the wrong boundary.

blocks.title: Mistake: making the whole page a Client Component
paragraphs: One interactive control does not mean the whole page needs 'use client'. Move the interaction down to the smallest sensible component and leave the rest on the server.

blocks.title: Mistake: fetching your own Route Handler from a Server Component
paragraphs: If both pieces run on your server, share the underlying function. Add HTTP when HTTP is part of the requirement, not as ceremony.

blocks.title: Mistake: assuming fetch is cached because an old tutorial said so
paragraphs: Caching defaults and APIs have changed across Next.js releases. Check the version and the Cache Components configuration before copying old examples.

blocks.title: Mistake: treating a layout redirect as authorisation
paragraphs: Redirecting unauthenticated users is useful UX. Protected operations still need permission checks at the server boundary that reads or writes the data.

blocks.title: Mistake: serialising independent data requests
paragraphs: If two reads do not depend on each other, start them together. Accidental waterfalls are one of the easiest ways to make a server-rendered route feel slow.

blocks.title: Mistake: confusing static rendering with browser cache TTL
paragraphs: A page can be statically generated and still ask the browser to revalidate its HTML. Rendering strategy and HTTP cache policy answer different questions.

blocks.title: Mistake: putting a secret in NEXT_PUBLIC_
paragraphs: Anything intentionally exposed to client code should be treated as public. Rename the variable only after deciding the value is safe for every visitor to see.

blocks.title: Mistake: adding Suspense boundaries everywhere
paragraphs: A boundary controls reveal order. Use it where a region can load independently without making the page harder to follow.

sections.title: Production checklist
sections.summary: A production checklist is useful because the last ten percent is mostly small things that are easy to forget and annoying to discover from users.

blocks.title: Before deployment
list: Run type checking, linting, tests, and a production build in CI.
Validate required environment configuration.
Keep secrets server-only.
Review large Client Component boundaries.
Check for obvious sequential data waterfalls.
Add loading, empty, error, and not-found states.
Confirm protected operations enforce authorisation on the server.
Check image dimensions and likely LCP resources.
Review third-party scripts.
Make important public routes reachable through internal links.

blocks.title: Search and sharing
list: Verify canonical URLs on the real domain.
Check robots.txt and sitemap.xml.
Give important routes unique titles and descriptions.
Test Open Graph images with absolute production URLs.
Use structured data only when it matches visible content.
Redirect retired URLs permanently where appropriate.

blocks.title: After deployment
list: Open the site from a clean browser session.
Inspect production response headers.
Verify authentication and permission boundaries.
Exercise one real mutation end to end.
Check error reporting.
Watch Web Vitals and slow requests.
Confirm caching and revalidation behave the way the product expects.
Test mobile navigation and keyboard navigation.

blocks.title: Prefer architecture you can explain
paragraphs: The best setup is rarely the one using the most Next.js features. It is the one where the next developer can tell what runs on the server, what reaches the browser, how fresh the data is, who may change it, and what happens when it fails.
If those answers are obvious from the code, the architecture is doing its job.

blocks.title: Deployments need a way back
paragraphs: A green build proves that the code compiled. It does not prove that production data, environment variables, third-party services, and real traffic will behave exactly as expected. Decide how to roll back before pressing deploy.

For database changes, prefer migrations that are compatible with both the old and new application for a short period. Add a nullable column before requiring it, deploy code that can handle both shapes, backfill the data, and only then tighten the constraint. This avoids turning a code rollback into a database emergency.
list: Keep the previous healthy deployment available.
Write down which changes cannot be rolled back safely.
Use feature flags for risky behaviour changes when possible.
Separate deployment success from feature release.
Test the rollback path occasionally, not during the first incident.

blocks.title: Run a small, real production smoke test
paragraphs: A useful smoke test follows one important journey with production URLs and production configuration. Sign in, load protected data, submit a harmless mutation, refresh the result, and sign out. That short path catches missing cookies, incorrect callback URLs, broken cache invalidation, and absent environment variables better than checking the home page alone.
Keep this test small enough that a person can run it after an urgent release. Automate it later, but first make sure the steps describe what healthy actually means for the product.
blocks.note: A status code of 200 is not the same thing as a working product. Test a journey that matters.

sections.title: Forms and validation
sections.summary: A good form works before JavaScript finishes loading, explains what went wrong, preserves useful input, and never trusts the browser as its security boundary.

blocks.title: Start with the form the browser already understands
paragraphs: HTML forms already know how to collect named fields and submit them. Server Actions fit that model well because a form can call server code through its action prop without building a separate client-side request layer first.

Use labels, names, sensible input types, autocomplete hints, and native constraints such as required where they help. Native validation is a useful first line of feedback, but the server must still validate every value. A request can be sent without your interface.

blocks.title: Parse untrusted input once on the server
paragraphs: FormData is intentionally loose. Fields may be missing, repeated, unexpectedly large, or shaped differently from what TypeScript suggests. Convert it into a domain object at the boundary and return clear field errors when parsing fails.

A schema library is helpful, but the important part is the boundary. The rest of the application should receive a known value such as CreateAccountInput, not raw FormData that gets interpreted differently in three places.
list: Trim text before checking minimum length.
Normalise email addresses only where your product rules allow it.
Reject unknown enum values rather than silently choosing a default.
Set size limits for text and uploaded files.
Return field errors for expected mistakes and throw only for unexpected failures.

blocks.title: Pending state should answer what happens next
paragraphs: When a submission begins, disable only the control that would create an accidental duplicate. Keep the rest of the page readable. A useful pending label says what is happening, such as Saving profile, instead of the vague Loading.
React form hooks can expose pending state and the result returned by a Server Action. Put status messages in a live region so screen-reader users hear the same feedback that sighted users see.
blocks.codeLabel: A submit button that understands its form

blocks.title: Use optimistic UI only when failure is easy to undo
paragraphs: A like button or a small reorder can feel instant with optimistic state. Payment, account deletion, and inventory reservation deserve a confirmed result. The question is not whether optimistic UI looks modern. The question is whether the interface can explain and recover from rejection without misleading the user.
Always keep a stable identifier for optimistic items, replace them with the server result, and remove or mark them when the write fails. Do not quietly leave invented state on screen.

blocks.title: Validation and permission checks solve different problems
paragraphs: Validation asks whether the input has an acceptable shape. Authorisation asks whether this user may perform the operation on this resource. A perfectly valid project ID is still dangerous if it belongs to somebody else.

Perform both checks inside the server operation. Then make the write idempotent where retries are possible, especially for payment callbacks, invitation acceptance, and other operations that should happen once.
blocks.note: Never use a hidden input as proof that a user owns the record named by that input.

sections.title: Environment and configuration
sections.summary: Configuration should fail clearly, keep secrets on the server, and make the differences between local, preview, and production environments deliberate.

blocks.title: Treat NEXT_PUBLIC values as published values
paragraphs: A variable prefixed with NEXT_PUBLIC can be included in browser JavaScript. Anybody can inspect it. Use that prefix for values that are meant to be public, such as an analytics site ID, never for a database password or a private API token.
Unprefixed variables are not automatically safe if you pass them into a Client Component or return them from an endpoint. Secrets stay private because your server code chooses not to expose them.

blocks.title: Fail at startup, not during the first real request
paragraphs: Reading process.env throughout the codebase spreads uncertainty. Create one server-only configuration module, validate required values, and export a typed object. A missing database URL should stop the build or boot process with a useful message.
This also gives tests a single place to provide controlled configuration and prevents small spelling differences from becoming runtime bugs.

blocks.title: Know whether a value is needed at build time or runtime
paragraphs: A statically generated page may read configuration while the application is building. A Route Handler may read it when a request arrives. That difference matters when one image is promoted through several environments or when secrets are injected only at runtime.
Document when each required value is consumed. If one build artifact must run in several environments, avoid baking environment-specific public values into that artifact unless that is intentional.

blocks.title: Preview should resemble production where it matters
paragraphs: Preview deployments are most useful when they exercise the same authentication flow, database shape, headers, and external integrations as production without sharing production data. A preview that silently disables half the system can only review appearance.

Use separate credentials and isolated data, but keep the integration boundaries realistic. Record intentional differences so a developer does not spend an afternoon debugging behaviour that was disabled by configuration.

blocks.title: Plan for secret rotation
paragraphs: Secrets eventually expire, leak, or need replacement. Know which deployment or service owns each secret and whether rotating it interrupts active sessions or callbacks.
When a provider supports overlapping keys, accept the old and new value during a short migration window. Rotate, verify traffic on the new key, then remove the old one.

sections.title: Accessibility in a routed application
sections.summary: Accessibility is part of navigation, loading, forms, and error recovery. It works best when it is built into the component contract instead of checked at the end.

blocks.title: Use the element that already has the behaviour
paragraphs: A button activates an action. A link moves to a location. A heading describes the structure beneath it. Choosing the correct element gives keyboard and assistive-technology behaviour without rebuilding it from div elements and event handlers.

Use ARIA to add missing context, not to disguise the wrong element. A div with role button still needs keyboard activation, focus styling, disabled behaviour, and every other detail a real button already provides.

blocks.title: Client navigation still needs a clear new-page experience
paragraphs: App Router navigation can replace content without a full browser load. Check where focus lands and whether the new page has a useful heading. A sighted user notices the content change immediately; a screen-reader user may need an announcement or a predictable focus target.
Keep a skip link near the beginning of the document and give the main region a stable id. This is especially valuable when a persistent header and documentation sidebar appear on every route.
blocks.code:
Skip to main content
{children}

blocks.title: Loading states should be calm and informative
paragraphs: Skeletons should preserve layout rather than flash dramatically. Avoid announcing every small streamed region as busy because a page with several Suspense boundaries can become noisy.

For an important action, expose a short status message and connect it to the relevant control. Respect reduced-motion preferences for orbital, parallax, and 3D effects. The experience should still make sense when animation is removed.

blocks.title: Drawers and dialogs must manage focus
paragraphs: When a mobile documentation drawer opens, focus should move into it. While it is open, keyboard focus should not disappear behind the overlay. Closing it should return focus to the button that opened it.

Escape should close a temporary overlay. Give the control an accessible name and expose its expanded state with aria-expanded. These details are small, but they decide whether the navigation can be used without a pointer.

blocks.title: Automated checks find only part of the problem
paragraphs: Lint rules and browser audits catch missing labels, invalid roles, and some contrast problems. They cannot tell whether the tab order is sensible or whether an error message is understandable.

Use the whole site with a keyboard. Zoom to 200 percent. Try a narrow viewport. Turn on reduced motion. Run at least one screen reader through the main journey. Fixing these problems usually improves the interface for everybody.

sections.title: Internationalisation and locale routing
sections.summary: Internationalisation affects URLs, metadata, formatting, caching, and layout. Decide the URL model before translating the first page.

blocks.title: Give each language a stable URL
paragraphs: A common App Router structure uses a dynamic locale segment such as app/[lang]. That makes language part of the URL, which helps links remain shareable and lets search engines understand each version as a distinct page.
Choose the supported locale list centrally. Reject unknown values with notFound instead of rendering a partly translated fallback under a URL that looks valid.
blocks.codeLabel: A locale segment at the root

blocks.title: Detection should help, not trap the visitor
paragraphs: The Accept-Language header can suggest a first language, but it should not override an explicit locale already present in the URL. Once a visitor chooses a language, remember the choice and keep the language switcher available.
Avoid redirect loops between a platform-level redirect and application locale detection. Pick one layer to own the initial decision and test requests with and without locale cookies.

blocks.title: Translate messages, but format values with locale-aware APIs
paragraphs: Dates, numbers, currencies, and plural rules should not be assembled with string concatenation. Intl.DateTimeFormat, Intl.NumberFormat, and Intl.PluralRules encode conventions that are easy to miss.
Keep raw values in data and format them near the presentation layer. A stored date should not become 09/10/2026 until the application knows which locale is reading it.

blocks.title: Metadata needs the same translation care as the page
paragraphs: Generate a translated title and description for every locale. Add alternate language URLs so search engines can connect equivalent pages, and make the canonical URL point to the current language version rather than always pointing to the default language.
Open Graph images may need translated text too. If one image is shared across languages, avoid embedding copy that contradicts the page title.

blocks.title: Design for text that changes shape
paragraphs: Translations are rarely the same length. Navigation labels grow, buttons wrap, and headings may need different line breaks. Test with long realistic strings rather than a made-up Lorem ipsum paragraph.

If right-to-left languages are supported, use logical CSS properties such as margin-inline and inset-inline. Check icons that imply direction, because an arrow that means next may need to flip while a familiar media-control icon may not.
blocks.note: Internationalisation is not a final translation pass. It is a routing and interface decision made early.

sections.title: Parallel and intercepted routes
sections.summary: Advanced routing is useful when several parts of a screen navigate independently or when a URL should open as an overlay during client navigation and as a full page on refresh.

blocks.title: Parallel routes give a layout named slots
paragraphs: A folder beginning with @ creates a slot that a parent layout receives as a prop. Slots do not become URL segments. They let one route compose independently rendered areas such as analytics, activity, and team panels.
Use this when the regions genuinely have separate navigation or loading behaviour. A normal component is simpler when the content always changes together.
blocks.codeLabel: A dashboard with two route slots
blocks.code:
app/dashboard/
├─ layout.tsx
├─ page.tsx
├─ @analytics/page.tsx
└─ @activity/page.tsx

export default function Layout({ children, analytics, activity }) {
  return <>{children}<aside>{analytics}</aside><section>{activity}</section></>
}

blocks.title: Every slot needs a sensible recovery path
paragraphs: During a soft navigation, Next.js can preserve the active subpage for a slot. After a full refresh, it needs a default.tsx when the current URL does not identify what that slot should render.
Treat default.tsx as an intentional fallback. Returning null is fine for an optional modal slot. A core dashboard panel should usually provide a useful default state.

blocks.title: Intercept a route when navigation context matters
paragraphs: An intercepted route can show a photo, sign-in form, or cart as a modal while preserving the page behind it. The same URL still renders as a normal page when it is opened directly or refreshed.
This solves a real product problem: the overlay has a shareable URL, browser back closes it naturally, and a direct visit never depends on the previous screen existing.
list: Use (.) for a route at the same segment level.
Use (..) for a route one segment above.
Remember that matchers count route segments, not folders such as @modal slots.
Keep the full-page route usable without the intercepted presentation.

blocks.title: A routed modal still has normal dialog responsibilities
paragraphs: Routing solves the URL and history behaviour. It does not provide focus trapping, Escape handling, an accessible name, scroll locking, or focus restoration. Use a tested dialog primitive or implement those behaviours deliberately.
Provide a close action that calls router.back when there is known navigation history, and a safe fallback route when the modal may have been reached in an unusual state.

blocks.title: Do not reach for advanced routing to avoid component state
paragraphs: Parallel and intercepted routes add file conventions that every future contributor must understand. They are worth it when the URL, browser history, reload behaviour, and independent loading states are part of the feature.
For a tooltip, disclosure, or temporary local panel, ordinary component state is usually the honest solution.

sections.title: Cookies, headers, and request data
sections.summary: Request data connects the browser to server rendering, but reading it changes when and where a route can be rendered. Use it close to the decision that needs it.

blocks.title: Request APIs are asynchronous and request-specific
paragraphs: In current Next.js, cookies and headers are asynchronous APIs. Their values only exist when a request arrives, so reading them opts the relevant route into dynamic work.
Do not read a cookie in the root layout simply because one deeply nested button needs it. That moves request-specific work higher in the tree and can remove useful prerendering opportunities.
blocks.codeLabel: Read a preference where it is used

blocks.title: Server Components read cookies, mutations write them
paragraphs: A Server Component can read cookies sent with the incoming request. It cannot set a cookie while rendering because response headers may already be streaming. Write or delete cookies in a Server Action or Route Handler.

Session cookies should normally use httpOnly, secure in production, an appropriate sameSite policy, an expiry, and a narrow path where possible. These flags reduce risk, but they do not replace session validation on the server.

blocks.title: Headers are useful context, not trusted identity
paragraphs: Headers can carry content negotiation, trace identifiers, forwarded host information, and platform metadata. Values supplied by the public internet are untrusted unless a trusted proxy overwrites and verifies them.

Never grant access because a caller sent x-user-role: admin. Authentication should establish identity through a verified session or token, then authorisation should load permissions from a trusted source.

blocks.title: Set broad response policy in configuration
paragraphs: Stable headers such as Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, and a carefully tested Content-Security-Policy are often clearer in next.config than repeated across handlers.
Route Handlers remain the right place for response-specific values such as a generated file name, webhook acknowledgement, or endpoint-specific cache policy.

blocks.title: Debug the complete request chain
paragraphs: When a cookie works locally but not in production, inspect domain, path, secure, sameSite, expiry, and the exact Set-Cookie response. When a host or protocol looks wrong, inspect the platform proxy headers and your trusted-host configuration.
Log names and decisions, not raw secrets. A trace can safely say that a session cookie was absent without printing the session value.

sections.title: Databases and data boundaries
sections.summary: Server Components can query a database directly. A clean data boundary keeps that convenience from spreading query details and permission mistakes across the component tree.

blocks.title: Skip an internal HTTP hop when the server owns both sides
paragraphs: A Server Component already runs on the server, so it can call a database function directly. Fetching your own Route Handler adds serialization, another error surface, and an HTTP round trip inside the same application.
Keep Route Handlers for real HTTP consumers such as mobile clients, webhooks, and public integrations. Share domain functions beneath both the page and the handler when they need the same operation.

blocks.title: Put permission-aware reads in a data access layer
paragraphs: A useful data function accepts the authenticated actor and the resource identifier, checks access, selects only the fields the caller needs, and returns a plain result. This makes the safe path the easy path.
Avoid returning a full database row to every component. An internal notes field or password hash can leak later when somebody spreads the object into a Client Component or JSON response.

blocks.title: Match connection strategy to the runtime
paragraphs: A long-running Node server, a serverless function, and an edge runtime have different connection limits and driver support. Use a database provider and driver designed for the environment where the query runs.
During local development, hot reload can recreate modules repeatedly. Follow the driver guidance for reusing clients so a small edit does not open a new pool until the database refuses connections.

blocks.title: Use a transaction when partial success would be wrong
paragraphs: Creating an order and decrementing inventory are one business operation even if they touch several tables. Put dependent writes in a transaction so either all of them commit or none do.

External calls cannot usually join the database transaction. Record durable intent, commit it, and let a retryable worker perform email, payment, or webhook work. This is more reliable than holding a database transaction open during a slow network call.

blocks.title: Observe queries before guessing about performance
paragraphs: Log slow query duration and inspect execution plans for important paths. Indexes help reads but add storage and write cost, so add them for actual access patterns rather than every column that looks searchable.
Pagination should have a stable order. For large or frequently changing collections, cursor pagination usually behaves more predictably than a deep offset.

sections.title: Instrumentation and tracing
sections.summary: Production debugging gets easier when logs, errors, traces, and Web Vitals describe the same request without exposing the person behind it.

blocks.title: Register server instrumentation once
paragraphs: Place instrumentation.ts at the project root, or beside app inside src when the project uses a src directory. Its register function runs when a server instance starts, before it begins handling requests.
Import runtime-specific packages inside register. A Node tracing library may not run in the edge runtime, and top-level imports can fail before your runtime check has a chance to help.

blocks.title: Capture server errors with useful context
paragraphs: The onRequestError hook can forward errors captured by the server to an observability provider. Include the route, operation, deployment version, and a correlation identifier. Avoid request bodies, cookies, access tokens, and personal fields by default.
A stack trace without release information tells you where code failed but not which code was running. Attach a commit SHA or deployment identifier to logs and error events.

blocks.title: Write logs that can answer a question
paragraphs: Structured logs are easier to filter than sentences assembled for the console. Use stable fields such as event, route, durationMs, status, requestId, and resourceId. Keep the human message short.
Choose log levels deliberately. A validation rejection is usually expected information, not an error page for the on-call engineer. A failed database connection is different.

blocks.title: Traces explain one request; metrics reveal a pattern
paragraphs: A trace connects the work inside a request: rendering, database queries, service calls, and cache access. Metrics show whether latency or failure rate changed across thousands of requests. Use both before deciding where a slowdown lives.
Measure product operations as well as framework internals. Checkout completion time or search failure rate is often more useful than a generic request average.

blocks.title: Alert on user impact, not every unusual event
paragraphs: An alert should ask for action. A brief increase in one harmless warning may belong on a dashboard, while sustained checkout failures should wake somebody up.
For every alert, write the likely causes, the first dashboard to open, and a safe mitigation. If nobody knows what to do when it fires, it is noise rather than protection.
